author: Akien
prose: i had typed you a reply about when i worked at broadcom, but it got lost. short of it: each commit kicked off most relevant tests. but not everything. an hourly test kinda like a broad smoke test ran. each evening, a full suite of everything but the longest running tests (40 hours). each friday evening, the whole suite. i am not saying we should follow this model, but perhaps there are useful ideas in it for our own testing. thoughts?
acted_on_note: CC 2026-09-07, answered in conversation (Fable session). The useful transfer from the Broadcom model is not the clock tiers but WHAT separated them: cost. Cairn is event-driven (event-not-poll), so the four tiers map onto events we already have or are casting: per-commit relevant tests = the seal horizon, made precise by ticket 675ab0daa171 (import-closure fingerprint: only proofs that load the edited file expire); hourly smoke = the at-rest probe on the beat (history_integrity already fires there); nightly-everything-but-slow = a re-seal of every expired seal EXCLUDING proofs above a declared cost band; Friday-full = the same with no exclusion. The one new thing that is worth building: a proof declares its cost band (ticket 0524c3b8b379 a-sieve-carries-its-band is the adjacent shape), so 'quick' is a declared budget and codemother's 600s proof is excluded by its own record rather than by a hand list. Not cast as a ticket today: it hangs on 675ab0daa171 and 1c4ae8f053fe landing first, since both change what a re-seal costs; revisit when they are PROVED.
